items.stem: A one-day 99% VaR model produces 12 exceptions in 250 trading days. What does this most likely indicate?

options.rationale: About 2-3 exceptions are expected at 99% over 250 days, not 12.

options.text: The model understates risk and fails backtesting
options.rationale: Correct: far more exceptions than expected signals the model underestimates risk.
Too many exceptions means under-, not over-statement.

options.text: Exceptions are irrelevant to VaR validation
options.rationale: Exception counts are the basis of VaR backtesting.

items.explanation: Correct: far more exceptions than expected signals the model underestimates risk.

items.stem: Expected loss on a loan is best expressed as:

options.rationale: Correct: expected loss is probability of default times loss given default times exposure at default.
The components are multiplied, not added.
This is not the expected-loss relationship.
LGD already reflects the recovery rate.

items.stem: Select TWO statements that correctly distinguish funding liquidity risk from market liquidity risk.

options.text: Funding liquidity risk is the risk of being unable to meet cash obligations as they fall due
options.rationale: Correct: funding liquidity concerns meeting obligations.

options.text: Market liquidity risk never affects asset prices
options.rationale: Market liquidity risk directly affects the price at which assets can be sold.

options.text: The two risks are identical in a stress event
options.rationale: They are distinct, though they can reinforce one another.

options.text: Market liquidity risk is the risk of being unable to sell an asset without a large price concession
options.rationale: Correct: that is the definition of market liquidity risk.

options.text: Funding liquidity risk only applies to equities
options.rationale: Funding liquidity risk is not asset-class specific.

items.explanation: Correct: funding liquidity concerns meeting obligations.
